rows.note: everything shares every core; PyTorch picks its own thread count
CONTROL: cap torch threads to the worker count, no pinning. The only difference from pinned_split is the affinity mask.
compute on cores [0, 1, 2, 3], decode on cores [4, 5, 6, 7] -- disjoint, strictly fewer each
both sides confined to cores [0, 1, 2, 3]. Same core COUNT as pinned_split, shared instead of disjoint -- so if these two tie, the effect is not partitioning.

separability_test_note: the two identical arms overlap as they must, so non-overlap elsewhere carries some weight -- at 7 repeats, not much.
noise_floor_note: PyTorch already defaulted to 4 threads on this 8-logical-core machine, so `default` and `threads_capped` are the same configuration measured twice. The 11.8% gap between their medians is therefore this benchmark's noise floor at 7 repeats, not an effect -- and every other number below has to clear it to mean anything.
verdict: pinning changes throughput by +41.3% against the thread-capped control, and the observed ranges do not overlap
disjointness_verdict: against pinned_half_shared -- same core count, shared rather than disjoint -- partitioning is worth +6.1%, but the ranges overlap, so any benefit of pinning here is not attributable to disjointness by this data
caveat: one laptop, one workload. The balance between contention removed and peak parallelism lost depends on the ratio of decode cost to compute cost, which is a property of this workload rather than of pinning.
